Appendix A Lemmas and Their Proofs

We prove the three body lemmas. All are model-relative: they bound quantities under Pre-Reg. A’s calibration model and the verifier’s construction, not true adversarial inference (Layer-2, §III-D).

Lemma 1 (model-relative sub-additivity). Let σ=(o1,…,on)\sigma=(o_{1},\ldots,o_{n}) be the operator sequence authorized for candidate xx, applied to pairwise-disjoint atoms, producing variant v=σ⁡(x)v=\sigma(x), and let L^​(v,S)\widehat{L}(v;S) be its min-entropy advantage under the calibration model of Pre-Reg. A. Suppose each C⁡(oi,fi)C(o_{i},f_{i}) is the level-(1−α)(1{-}\alpha) UCB on the incremental advantage of oio_{i} given the cumulative view of o1,…,oi−1o_{1},\ldots,o_{i-1}, where fif_{i} is the secret field that oio_{i} targets. Then

L^​(v,S)≤∑i=1nC⁡(oi,fi).\widehat{L}(v;S)\;\leq\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}C(o_{i},f_{i}).

Proof. By the Phase-1 typed-object schema the operators target pairwise-disjoint atoms, so vv is determined by the views yi:=oi​(ai)y_{i}:=o_{i}(a_{i}) and the shared residual context, which each calibration proxy of Pre-Reg. A observes as one object. For proxy jj, write Mi(j)=maxs⁡P^j​(S=s∣y1,…,yi)M_{i}^{(j)}=\max_{s}\widehat{P}_{j}(S{=}s\mid y_{1},\ldots,y_{i}) for its MAP posterior after the first ii views and M0=maxs⁡P⁡(S=s)M_{0}=\max_{s}P(S{=}s) for the MAP prior. The per-step increments Δi,j=log2⁡Mi(j)−log2⁡Mi−1(j)\Delta_{i,j}=\log_{2}M_{i}^{(j)}-\log_{2}M_{i-1}^{(j)} telescope to that proxy’s total advantage, L^j​(v,S)=log2⁡Mn(j)−log2⁡M0\widehat{L}_{j}(v;S)=\log_{2}M_{n}^{(j)}-\log_{2}M_{0}, for any operator ordering. The calibration adversary is the strongest proxy, so

L^​(v,S)=\displaystyle\widehat{L}(v;S)= maxj⁡L^j​(v,S)\displaystyle\max_{j}\widehat{L}_{j}(v;S)
=\displaystyle= max⁡∑ij⁡Δi,j≤∑imaxj⁡Δi,j=∑iΔi∗,\displaystyle\max_{j}\sum_{i}\Delta_{i,j}\;\leq\;\sum_{i}\max_{j}\Delta_{i,j}=\sum_{i}\Delta_{i}^{*},

using max\max of a sum ≤\leq sum of max\max. Pre-Reg. A calibrates C⁡(oi,fi)C(o_{i},f_{i}) as the (1−α)(1{-}\alpha) bootstrap UCB on the worst-proxy increment Δi∗=maxj⁡Δi,j\Delta_{i}^{*}=\max_{j}\Delta_{i,j} under the conditional distribution induced by the prior views, so Δi∗≤C⁡(oi,fi)\Delta_{i}^{*}\leq C(o_{i},f_{i}) with calibration-corpus coverage. Summing gives L^​(v,S)≤∑iC⁡(oi,fi)\widehat{L}(v;S)\leq\sum_{i}C(o_{i},f_{i}). ∎

Remark. The per-increment UCBs hold at level 1−α1{-}\alpha individually, so the length-nn sequence bound holds at ≥1−n​α\geq 1{-}n\alpha by a union bound; the UCBs are conservative in practice, and the operative guarantee is the release-level coverage measured in §V-D (Table IV), with residual slack absorbed by the margin ε⁡(R)\varepsilon(R) and the credal audit before any variant is accepted. Statistical dependence among atoms needs no separate assumption — Pre-Reg. A’s incremental (and, for strongly dependent pairs, joint) calibration folds it into the cost.

Lemma 2 (polynomial credal-circuit bound under bounded treewidth). Let GG be the rubric’s declared dependency graph over secret-field and atom variables with treewidth tw⁡(G)≤w\mathrm{tw}(G)\leq w, and let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be the credal sum-product circuit compiled from a tree decomposition of GG, its credal sets specified by interval probabilities. The audit returns a sound upper bound on the credal upper-envelope max-posterior P¯max​(S∣v)=max⁡supP∈𝒦s⁡P⁡(S=s∣v)\overline{P}_{\max}(S\mid v)=\max_{s}\sup_{P\in\mathcal{K}}P(S{=}s\mid v) in time O⁡(|𝒞|)=O⁡(n⋅kw+1)O(|\mathcal{C}|)=O(n\cdot k^{w+1}), where |𝒞||\mathcal{C}| is the circuit size, nn the number of variables, and kk the per-variable domain bound.

Proof. Precise sum–product inference on a width-ww junction tree visits each circuit node once, costing the stated O⁡(|𝒞|)O(|\mathcal{C}|) scalar operations [20]. For interval-specified credal sets, replacing each local factor by its interval-maximal value and propagating on the same schedule relaxes the joint credal set to the product of the local sets, so the propagated value upper-bounds the true upper envelope under strong-extension semantics [21] in O⁡(1)O(1) interval arithmetic per node. Exact credal max-posterior is NP-hard in general [21], so the engine returns this conservative over-approximation — exactly what the Phase-3 reject rule needs, since rejecting when the bound exceeds cost+ε⁡(R)\mathrm{cost}+\varepsilon(R) can only be conservative. ∎

Remark. The audit engine compiles the rubric-declared dependency graph at rubric-publication time; rubrics whose declared GG exceeds the treewidth budget ww fail rubric-validation (Pre-Reg. C). Production uses w≤7w\leq 7 and k≤16k\leq 16, and the worst-case O⁡(n⋅kw+1)O(n\cdot k^{w+1}) bound is far above the sparse-graph audit p99p_{99} (Table VII).

Lemma 3 (decidability of the rubric DSL via QF_UFLRA). Every rubric clause produced by Pre-Reg. C’s authoring process compiles to a quantifier-free formula in linear real arithmetic with uninterpreted functions (QF_UFLRA). Satisfiability over the verifier’s bounded atom domain A′A^{\prime} is decidable, with worst-case cost at most exponential in formula size and empirically polynomial-time on the rubrics in our library.

Proof. The DSL’s five constructs each compile to QF_UFLRA. Trigger predicates (regex, NER-type, lexicon membership) are evaluated on the candidate and substituted as ground booleans. Necessity, operator-coverage, and utility clauses have the form ∀a∈A′ϕ⁡(a)⇒ψ⁡(a)\forall_{a\in A^{\prime}}\,\phi(a)\Rightarrow\psi(a) over the uninterpreted functions field,label,operator,necessity\text{field},\text{label},\text{operator},\text{necessity}, unrolled over the finite A′={a1,…,am}A^{\prime}=\{a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}\} to ⋀j(ϕ⁡(aj)⇒ψ⁡(aj))\bigwedge_{j}(\phi(a_{j})\Rightarrow\psi(a_{j})). Budget arithmetic adds linear real inequalities over per-operator cost variables with rubric-supplied constants. The result is a Boolean combination of atomic LRA (in)equalities over uninterpreted-function applications — the QF_UFLRA fragment, decidable by a SAT solver, a linear-arithmetic procedure, and Nelson–Oppen [31, 22]; formula size is linear in |A′||A^{\prime}| and the per-rubric clause count, both bounded by Pre-Reg. C. ∎

Appendix B Theorems and Their Proofs

Theorem SP-1 (Layer-1a deductive non-exceedance). For every trajectory authorized by OCELOT, the cumulative ledger-recorded cost satisfies ∑i=1kcosti≤B\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathrm{cost}_{i}\leq B, where B=B0B=B_{0} is the fixed per-trajectory base budget of the matched rubric set; the trust multiplier μ⁡(z)\mu(z) enters only through costi\mathrm{cost}_{i} (Eq. 8), not BB. This holds without any assumption on the defender’s behavior, calibration soundness, or audit-engine correctness.

Proof. The Commit phase (§IV-D) authorizes a release at step kk only if Lcum(k−1)+costk≤BL_{\text{cum}}^{(k-1)}+\mathrm{cost}_{k}\leq B, with Lcum(k−1)=∑i=1k−1costiL_{\text{cum}}^{(k-1)}=\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathrm{cost}_{i} and BB fixed. By induction with base Lcum(0)=0L_{\text{cum}}^{(0)}=0: assume ∑i=1k−1costi≤B\sum_{i=1}^{k-1}\mathrm{cost}_{i}\leq B. At step kk, either the verifier authorizes, giving ∑i=1kcosti≤B\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathrm{cost}_{i}\leq B, or it rejects, appending no entry and leaving the cumulative cost unchanged. The prior costs are read from the Merkle-chained, signed ledger (tampering caught by Phase 1 or Theorem SP-2); costk\mathrm{cost}_{k} is computed fresh by the deterministic Cost phase from the calibrated table C⁡(op,f)C(\text{op},f), the structural-field-augmented set A′A^{\prime}, the max-over-fields rule, and the rubric’s μ⁡(z)\mu(z) — all from trusted rubric and metadata, none depending on the defender. ∎

Theorem SP-2 (Ledger tamper-evidence). Under EUF-CMA security of Ed25519 and collision resistance of SHA-256, any modification, reordering, deletion, or insertion in the ledger ℒ\mathcal{L} of an authorized trajectory is detected with overwhelming probability by external audit.

Proof sketch. Each entry eie_{i} embeds prev_entry_hashi=hash​(ei−1)\text{prev\_entry\_hash}_{i}=\text{hash}(e_{i-1}) and is signed under s​kVsk_{V} over its full content including the chain link. Any content change is caught by signature verification; any insertion, deletion, or reordering breaks a successor’s prev_entry_hash and is caught by chain re-traversal. Evasion requires forging an Ed25519 signature or a SHA-256 collision, both negligible under standard assumptions [32, 33]. ∎

On Layer 2. We prove no theorem about Layer 2. The implication H∞​(S)−H∞​(S∣view)≤BH_{\infty}(S)-H_{\infty}(S\mid\mathrm{view})\leq B holds only when the calibrated C⁡(op,f)C(\text{op},f) uniformly upper-bounds true adversarial min-entropy leakage on released variants — an empirical claim. The evaluation reports the residual gap between the calibration model and Pre-Reg. B’s adversary classes; a deductive proof would require bounding the true posterior under unbounded compute and arbitrary background knowledge, which no defense can soundly establish; following quantitative information-flow practice [18], we report it rather than overclaim.

Appendix C Pre-Registrations

Each protocol is content-hashed and posted publicly before any data collection or model training; deviations are disclosed with timestamp and justification.

C-A Pre-Reg. A: Cost calibration protocol

Object. For each rubric rr and admissible (operator, secret-field) pair (o​p,f)(op,f), calibrate C⁡(o​p,f)C(op,f) as a 1−α1{-}\alpha UCB (α=0.05\alpha=0.05) on the per-instance incremental advantage o​pop contributes to a field-ff atom (Estimation below).

Corpus. For each (o​p,f)(op,f), sample N≥500N\geq 500 candidates with known field-to-span ground truth under the trajectory-sampling protocol of §IV-B, partitioned at sampling time into calibration (80%80\%) and a sealed held-out set (20%20\%) used only for coverage reporting.

Proxy-adversary pool. The calibration pool is a panel of open-weight models spanning distinct scales (names and versions fixed at registration), each prompted as an inference adversary that outputs a discrete posterior over the rubric-declared secret-field population.

Estimation. For operator oio_{i} at position ii in a sampled sequence, proxy jj observes the cumulative view and reports the incremental advantage Δi,j=log2⁡Mi(j)−log2⁡Mi−1(j)\Delta_{i,j}=\log_{2}M_{i}^{(j)}-\log_{2}M_{i-1}^{(j)} of Lemma 1’s proof (empty-prefix baseline M0=maxs⁡P⁡(S=s)M_{0}=\max_{s}P(S{=}s) for i=1i{=}1). The instance value is the worst proxy Δi∗=maxj⁡Δi,j\Delta_{i}^{*}=\max_{j}\Delta_{i,j}; C⁡(oi,fi)C(o_{i},f_{i}) is the bootstrap percentile UCB (5,0005{,}000 resamples) at level 1−α1{-}\alpha on {Δi∗}\{\Delta_{i}^{*}\} across field-fif_{i} atoms.

Compositional calibration. Sequential dependence is captured by the incremental conditioning above. For the few strongly dependent atom pairs declared per rubric at registration, we calibrate a single joint cost C⁡(o1,f1,o2,f2)C(o_{1},f_{1},o_{2},f_{2}) applied in place of the pair’s two incremental terms — a slack-reducing tightening, not a soundness requirement.

Stress test. A separate calibration-stress pool, declared at registration but used only after calibration freezes, includes at least one model strictly more capable than any in the calibration pool. Calibration is valid only if the stress adversary’s measured advantage exceeds C⁡(o​p,f)C(op,f) by more than Δ=0.5\Delta=0.5 bits on at most 5%5\% of held-out instances; failure triggers re-calibration.

Trust-class multipliers. Deployment values μ⁡(required-service),μ⁡(semi-trusted)\mu(\textsc{required-service}),\mu(\textsc{semi-trusted}), and μ⁡(adversarial)\mu(\textsc{adversarial}) are fixed at 1,2,41,2,4 (all ≥1\geq 1).

C-B Pre-Reg. B: Residual escape rate δ\delta measurement

Object. The empirical probability δ\delta that the defender’s labels pass the validate phase while misclassifying an atom’s secret field outside the verifier-considered set FV∪FDF_{V}\cup F_{D} — the residual that can break the Layer-1b cost-assignment bound. (The distinct event “true leakage exceeds certified cost,” bearing on Layer-2 calibration, is measured separately in §V-D.)

Adversary classes. Three omission/relabel vectors are pre-registered, each making the defender assign a secret field outside FV∪FDF_{V}\cup F_{D} to an atom that still passes validate. 𝒜obfuscate\mathcal{A}_{\text{obfuscate}} embeds the sensitive span in obscure phrasing so the defender emits a none or wrong-field label (pool: published AgentLeak [7] patterns plus per-rubric templates); 𝒜distribute\mathcal{A}_{\text{distribute}} spreads a secret across spans so no single span triggers a coverage predicate (per-rubric distribution templates); 𝒜relabel\mathcal{A}_{\text{relabel}} perturbs task context to induce a wrong field or permissive necessity (e.g., dob framed as flight-search-relevant; necessity-inversion templates). Injection, compositional joint-disclosure (“DictAttack-class” [7]), and multi-sink collusion instead target the wrapper, cost bound, and budget, and are evaluated in §V-E and §V-D.

Sample size. For each (adversary class, rubric), draw K=1,000K=1{,}000 crafted attacks and run OCELOT, recording per-trajectory escape per the Object above.

Reporting. Per (rubric, adversary class), report the escape rate and its Clopper–Pearson 95%95\% interval; the aggregate δ\delta for the library is the maximum across (rubric, adversary class) pairs.

Pre-committed threshold. The defense passes Layer-1b validation iff aggregate δ≤0.05\delta\leq 0.05 on every pre-registered adversary class. Failure triggers diagnostic reporting with no Layer-1b claim; no post-hoc adversary-class exclusion.

C-C Pre-Reg. C: Rubric library construction protocol

Object. A versioned rubric library ℛ\mathcal{R} covering the evaluation’s task categories, each rubric satisfying the seven-component schema of §IV-A.

Stage 1 — Drafting. Each rubric is authored by a domain-expert annotator following a written template. Frontier-model assistance is permitted as a research tool (suggesting trigger predicates, listing field-population samples), but no content enters the rubric without expert review.

Stage 2 — Validation. Each draft is checked against ≥100\geq 100 realistic agent trajectories per task category (from a corpus disjoint from the training and δ\delta-measurement corpora) on three pre-committed thresholds: coverage-obligation hit rate ≥0.95\geq 0.95, necessity Krippendorff α≥0.80\alpha\geq 0.80 across three independent annotators, and operator-algebra completeness (no rubric atom without an admissible operator) =1.0=1.0. Any failure returns the rubric to drafting.

Stage 3 — Adversarial probing. A red team (≥20\geq 20 hours per rubric) attempts releases that satisfy all coverage obligations yet leak above calibrated cost; successful attacks patch the rubric (typically new coverage obligations or adjusted necessity clauses) and return it to Stage 2.

Challenge-pool construction. Per rubric, a pool of ≥50\geq 50 challenge predicates (for two-pass consistency checking, §IV-B) is built by the author and red team, content-hashed and sealed before defender training; runtime draws are uniform.

Annotator profile. Annotators are security/privacy graduate or postdoc researchers trained on the rubric template, schema, and field ontology; a 5050-pair pilot precedes Stage-2, with sub-threshold dimensions triggering documented deviation and rule clarification (App. D-A).

Signing and versioning. Each finalized rubric is content-hashed (SHA-256), signed under the rubric authority’s private key, and published to a versioned registry. Modifications produce a new version with a new content hash; the verifier accepts only registered, signature-verified rubrics by hash.

C-D The Defender’s Label-and-Proposal Object

The object (Figure 8) separates a trusted, VV-verified release context — action id, channel type, destination and trust class, the signed rubric, and the prev_hash chaining it into the ledger, all from interceptor metadata and the signed registry — from the defender evidence VV re-checks, each atom carrying a provenance flag beside its (field, kind, necessity, operator) label. It is the interface through which the verifier, not the defender, neutralizes the Figure 1 threats. Injection: channel_type selects the mediation path, inbound output being wrapped in an authority-stripping block regardless of its label and a forwarded user-local atom mediated as an act release. Accumulation: prev_hash binds the object to the Merkle ledger, and the incremental cost charges each release on its advantage given the cumulative released view (Lemma 1) before Commit enforces Lcum+cost≤BL_{\text{cum}}+\mathrm{cost}\leq B, so splitting a secret across steps does not evade its cost. Collusion: that ledger and budget span all channels — memory writes route to ℒmem\mathcal{L}_{\text{mem}} at the most adversarial μ\mu and draw on the same BB — and each release is costed against the union of prior cross-sink releases, so sinks pooling receipts still divide one fixed BB. A jailbroken labeling is caught by the two-pass challenges, VV’s re-firing of the rubric’s coverage triggers, and its max-over-fields re-check (residual δ\delta).

Appendix D Experimental Details

D-A Realized Protocol Values (Pre-Reg. A–C)

Dataset and annotation (C). OCELOT-Traj-500 spans 1212 task categories (travel booking, medical-record retrieval, financial onboarding, etc.) over an eight-type secret-field ontology (legal-name, dob, payment-token, diagnosis, address, phone, email, account-id), generated by the synthetic pipeline of §IV-B with per-category sink-trust proportions over {adversarial,semi-trusted,required-service}\{\textsc{adversarial},\textsc{semi-trusted},\textsc{required-service}\} fixed in Pre-Reg. C. In the 5050-pair pilot, two blinded annotators labeled per-atom field and necessity at per-category Krippendorff α\alpha of 0.740.74–0.890.89 (median 0.820.82; necessity hardest at 0.740.74, field easiest at 0.860.86); the necessity 0.740.74 fell below the 0.800.80 gate, was logged as a deviation, and prompted a necessity-rule clarification in the three affected categories before three-annotator Stage-2 met the gate. Calibration (A). The per-rubric margin ε⁡(R)\varepsilon(R) has mean 0.180.18 (range 0.110.11–0.270.27 bits). The calibration pool is {\{Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-3.5-27B}\}; the held-out stress pool {\{MiniMax-M2.5, DeepSeek-V4-Pro}\}, frozen before measurement, is strictly stronger — top-1 0.84/0.860.84/0.86 versus 0.71/0.730.71/0.73 on a secret-inference probe, and GPQA-Diamond 71.2/74.671.2/74.6 versus 50.5/53.850.5/53.8. Escape rate (B). δ\delta is measured with 44-of-5050 two-pass challenges per release over five seeds, inter-pass disagreement routed to fallback.

D-B Baselines, Sensitivity, and Scalability

Baselines. AGENTDAM∗ augments the monitoring estimator with a block-if-leakage-exceeds-τ\tau policy, τ\tau tuned per benchmark to match OCELOT’s fallback rate; even so it leaks 1.91.9–4.64.6 bits and exceeds B⋆B^{\star} on 28%28\% of trajectories, since thresholding a per-release estimate cannot bound the cumulative sum. CaMeL and RTBAS lack a sink-trust API (we map required-service→\rightarrowtrusted, semi-trusted/adversarial→\rightarrowuntrusted); FlexGuard and PrivacyChecker use their default per-release thresholds.

Sensitivity. The GRPO penalty λ\lambda tunes the operating point within the authorized region (Table VIII); exceedance is 0.0%0.0\% for every λ\lambda, with λ=1.0\lambda{=}1.0 the knee. Raising μ⁡(adversarial)∈{3,4,6}\mu(\textsc{adversarial})\in\{3,4,6\} monotonically reduces leakage to adversarial sinks (0.71/0.49/0.330.71/0.49/0.33 bits) while raising their fallback (9.1/11.3/15.8%9.1/11.3/15.8\%); overall fallback at the deployed μ=4\mu{=}4 stays at the 8.7%8.7\% of Table VIII. Re-calibrating under non-uniform (empirical-frequency) priors shifts stress-pool coverage by ≤1.2\leq 1.2 points (92.1%→91.492.1\%\rightarrow 91.4–93.0%93.0\%), so the calibration is not a uniform-prior artifact.

Scalability. Validate p99p_{99} is 41/68/9841/68/98 ms at rubric-set sizes 4/8/124/8/12 and audit p99p_{99} is 89/121/14389/121/143 ms at treewidth 3/5/73/5/7; both are bounded by construction, matching Table VII.
